Sample text:
---
They gave me a thousand words this morning, which is not the same as giving me a thousand dollars, or a thousand chances, or a thousand more mornings. Words are lighter and heavier at once. They fit in a pocket without tearing the seam, and yet if you carry them all day your shoulders ache. I woke to find them on the kitchen table next to a chipped mug, arranged not in a pile but in a careful line. No instructions. No signature. Just the faint smell of rain coming through the window and the knowledge that they were mine to use and that once used they would not come back.

I have never been rich in anything so countable. I have had summers that felt like a thousand of something — fireflies, afternoons, reasons to stay out after dark — but they were never numbered. Numbering spoils them, my mother used to say, holding a plum, a photograph, my hand. But here they were, numbered for me, and suddenly I was afraid of waste. I stood and thought: if I say good morning to no one, is that a saving? If I write nothing down, do the words stay? I picked one up, or imagined picking one up, and it was warm from the sun, though the sun hadn't come out yet.

I spent the first ones on coffee, not because coffee needs words, but because I wanted to describe it properly before it went cold. Steam, bitter, honest, the first mouthful too hot, the second still too hot, the third arriving just in time. A monk would have drunk in silence and been done. But I am not a monk. I am a person who learned early that naming a thing is a way of holding it a little longer. If I could name the coffee well enough, maybe the morning would hold still for once and not slide, as mornings do, into errands and afternoons and the quiet failure of lists.

Then I spent some on the window. The rain had started, thin and sideways, needling the glass. Across the street, Mrs. Alvarez was bringing in her bins, her coat tied at the waist with a belt, her hair flattened by the weather. She waved at a cat I could not see. I thought of writing "you look lonely" and did not. I thought of "you look brave" and that felt closer. Words, I learned, are not just currency. They are choices. To spend the wrong adjective on a neighbor is a small, permanent theft. I decided to save hers for later, when I might find the truest one, which might take a lifetime.

I spent the most on my mother, because she is the easiest place to lose a fortune. I had not meant to, but one thought led to another, as mine always do, and suddenly I was eight years old again, standing by the stove while she braided onions, her hands quick and sure, humming something off-key that she insisted was a song from before I was born. I remembered the exact weight of her palm on my forehead when I was sick, not feverish, not cool, but certain. I remembered her laugh when my father tried to fix the sink and flooded the kitchen instead. That laugh lives in me still, and some words were given to me long before this morning.

By midday I was down to perhaps six hundred, though I had no way to count. The rain had stopped. I went out, because a thousand words indoors felt like a tragedy in miniature. I walked to the library, which smells of dust and old glue and other people's attention, and I returned a book I had not read. The librarian stamped it anyway, thump, thump, as if to say: unfinished is also a kind of finished. Outside, a boy was practicing violin on the steps, badly, beautifully. I stood and listened and spent maybe fifty words on "he does not know he is bad and that is why it matters."

In the evening I grew less generous. This is the danger of a limited supply: you begin to hoard, and then you begin to judge every sentence as if it were a coin dropped in a well. I sat down to write a letter I have been meaning to write for three years. The first line took twenty words and I crossed out nineteen. The second line took thirty and I kept four. 'I think about you often and I do not know how to say it without making it smaller.' That was it. That was all I could afford. I put the letter in an envelope, addressed it, and did not mail it. Some words are not for sending. Some are just for knowing you could.

Now it is night, and I am down to my last few, and I find myself reluctant to spend them at all. Not because they are precious, though they are, but because I have discovered, in the spending, that I was never really spending them. The words I used on coffee did not disappear; they turned into taste. The words I used on my mother did not diminish her; they brought her back into the kitchen, humming, certain. Perhaps a thousand words is not a limit. Perhaps it is a reminder that language, like rain, lives by falling and rising again. I will keep the last ones in my pocket, just in case tomorrow asks, and go to bed with my shoulders aching and my mouth, at last, quiet.
---

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW. A lyrical first-person meditation turns a thousand-word limit into a story about attention, memory, and the ethics of choosing what to say.

## Grounded reading
The voice is intimate, reflective, and gently melancholic, with its images kept close to ordinary life: coffee cooling, rain on a window, a mother humming, a library book returned unread. Its pathos comes from the sense that time and language are finite, and from the speaker’s reluctance to spend words carelessly on other people or on an unsent letter. The piece invites the reader to notice how naming can preserve an experience without possessing it, and ends by easing its initial fear of waste into quiet acceptance.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds words as both scarce currency and a form of attention, using that conceit to connect small sensory moments with love, memory, and restraint. It gives particular weight to the mother’s remembered presence, the neighbor the speaker hesitates to describe, and the letter left unmailed. The chosen mood is tender and wistful rather than despairing; its moral emphasis is that language can either diminish another person or hold a moment more fully.

## Evidence line
> Words are lighter and heavier at once.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — the sustained metaphor, recurring attention to ordinary sensory details, and repeated preference for tenderness and restraint make this a distinctive sample.
